steps.title: Many styles
steps.body: Pinotage is made in several styles. Light and fruity, for early drinking. Coffee Pinotage, a 2000s trend, aged with heavily toasted oak for mocha and chocolate notes. Serious, structured wines from old vines, aged in French oak. And rosé, even sparkling and fortified versions.

steps.title: Reputation
steps.body: In the 1990s, critics complained of acetone and burnt rubber smells in some Pinotage. Research linked these to isoamyl acetate and to fermentation at high temperatures, stressed yeast and over-extraction. Better vineyard work, cooler fermentations and gentle handling have greatly improved quality.

steps.prompt: What caused the acetone notes in some 1990s Pinotage?
steps.explanation: High fermentation temperatures and stressed yeast created volatile compounds; modern winemaking avoids them.

steps.title: The Cape blend
steps.body: A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of Pinotage, usually 30 to 70%, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Shiraz. It gives South Africa a distinctive blend of its own, combining Pinotage's fruit with Bordeaux grapes' structure. Many Stellenbosch estates make one.
steps.highlight: Cape blend: Pinotage plus Bordeaux grapes

steps.prompt: A Cape blend is a red blend with a significant share of ____.
steps.explanation: Pinotage gives Cape blends their South African identity.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Pinotage ranges from light and fruity to serious and oaked
Old faults came from winemaking, now largely fixed
Cape blends combine Pinotage with Bordeaux grapes
